title: The Perfect Window

scenario.situation: A strategy shows outsized returns over a chosen 18-month backtest window.
scenario.stakeholderBelief: The desk wants to deploy capital immediately, citing the strong backtest as proof the strategy works.
scenario.question: Is the 18-month backtest sufficient evidence to deploy capital?

decisions.prompt: The desk is eager to deploy. How do you structure the investigation before signing off?

options.label: Verify the backtest calculations
options.detail: Re-run the same 18-month window to confirm the numbers are correct.
options.consequence: The numbers check out — the backtest is arithmetically accurate. But you've only confirmed what the desk already showed you. You haven't learned whether the window is representative or cherry-picked.
options.divergenceCost: Anchored entirely on the chosen window and confirmed the desk's framing instead of challenging it.

options.label: Rolling-window and out-of-sample diagnostic
options.detail: Run the strategy across ALL available historical windows and hold out a recent period untouched during development.
options.consequence: Expanding the frame immediately reveals that the 18-month window is an outlier — most rolling windows show near-zero or negative returns, and the out-of-sample period confirms the pattern doesn't persist.

options.label: Stress-test the chosen window
options.detail: Apply scenario shocks (e.g., vol spikes) to the 18-month period to see how returns behave under stress.
options.consequence: Stress tests within the same window show the strategy is somewhat robust to simulated shocks — but you're still inside the charmed period. Window selection bias is invisible from inside the window.
options.divergenceCost: Stress-tested inside the cherry-picked window, missing the selection bias entirely.

options.label: Benchmark the Sharpe ratio against peers
options.detail: Compare the strategy's Sharpe ratio over the 18-month window to industry benchmarks.
options.consequence: The Sharpe looks impressive versus benchmarks — but both the strategy and the benchmark are evaluated over the same hand-picked favorable period. Relative ranking doesn't expose absolute window bias.
options.divergenceCost: Compared within the same biased window, letting the cherry-pick contaminate the benchmark comparison too.

decisions.prompt: You've run the strategy across multiple windows. Which metric do you trust to assess true performance?

artifact.title: Annualized return by selected favorable windows
artifact.caption: Returns look strong when you pick windows that worked. Is this representative performance, or performance that was selected because it looked good?

options.label: Best-window annualized return
options.detail: Report the annualized return from the strongest-performing backtest window.
options.consequence: The headline number looks compelling — but picking the best window is precisely the bias you're trying to detect. Reporting it gives the desk the number they want, not the number they need.
options.divergenceCost: Selected the best-performing window as the evidence — maximizing the bias instead of diagnosing it.

options.label: Return distribution across all rolling windows plus out-of-sample return
options.detail: Summarize mean, median, and spread of returns across every rolling window, and separately report the out-of-sample holdout return.
options.consequence: The distribution exposes the truth: the 18-month window sits in the far right tail, the median rolling return is near zero, and the out-of-sample period shows negative performance. The strategy's edge evaporates outside the chosen window.

artifact.title: Annualized return across ALL rolling 18-month windows + out-of-sample
artifact.caption: The chosen window is an outlier in the right tail. The out-of-sample period — never touched during development — confirms the strategy has no persistent edge.

decisions.prompt: Rolling windows show near-zero median returns and the out-of-sample period is negative. What do you tell the desk?

options.label: "This strategy doesn't work — kill it."
options.detail: Declare the strategy without merit and recommend abandoning it.
options.consequence: Blunt and defensible — but you've made an overconfident negative call. It's possible the strategy has a real but narrow regime; you've foreclosed that inquiry and given the desk no path forward, reducing the chance they engage with the findings constructively.
options.divergenceCost: Overclaimed a negative conclusion with the same certainty the desk overclaimed a positive one.

options.label: "The chosen window is a right-tail outlier; rolling and out-of-sample results show no persistent edge — we need regime-conditioned testing and a live paper-trade period before committing capital."
options.detail: Present the distributional finding, flag the window selection problem, and propose a structured path to genuine validation.
options.consequence: The desk sees the full distribution, understands why the 18-month number is misleading, and has a concrete next step. You've protected the firm from premature deployment while keeping the door open if the strategy survives rigorous testing.

insight: The strategy's impressive backtest was an artifact of window selection — the 18-month period happened to capture a favorable regime, and the researcher implicitly searched for it. The real signal emerged only when returns were measured across every rolling window and an untouched out-of-sample holdout: median performance was near zero, and out-of-sample was negative. The lesson is researcher degrees of freedom: the more a window can be chosen after observing results, the less the backtest means — and the only credible evidence is performance on data that was never seen during development.
